records.title: Three Ways to Add a Custom Tool
records.contentHtml: From an actor’s Capabilities drawer you can add Execute Code (sandboxed Python for calculations), Execute Workflow (kick off another Acme workflow and optionally wait for the result), or an HTTP Request (call an internal or third-party API), all without any canvas wiring.

records.title: Scope Integrations Down to the Actions an Actor Needs
records.contentHtml: When you wire an integration into an actor’s Capabilities, expose only the specific actions it needs, like just send-email, rather than a whole app’s action list. Give an actor “all of Gmail” and it may call delete-thread when a user says “delete this conversation.”

records.title: Free-Form by Default, Scripted When It Must Be Exact
records.contentHtml: Actors are free-form by default, deciding what to say turn by turn, and that is right most of the time. Switch to the Advanced tab’s step builder only when you need an exact, repeatable sequence, like a payment flow or identity check; scripts longer than about 8 steps are usually better split into multiple actors.

records.title: Slots Carry Data Across Handoffs Automatically
records.contentHtml: Values collected by Ask Question steps, such as a name, an email, or an order number, are saved to slots that survive every actor transfer for the life of the conversation. By default every actor’s prompt includes a “Collected information so far” summary, so users never repeat themselves.

records.title: Not Every Channel Works Both Ways
records.contentHtml: Widget is inbound-only, since there is no one to start a conversation with an anonymous visitor, while SMS and WhatsApp Business are outbound-only. Gmail, Outlook, Slack, Teams, and Phone support both inbound and outbound, so check the channel matrix before wiring a channel to an Initiator flow.

records.title: Execution Mode Is Set on the Flow, Not on a Node
records.contentHtml: Responder or Initiator is chosen once per flow in Flow settings, not configured through a separate dispatcher node. Responder flows wait for inbound messages; Initiator flows are started manually, from a workflow, or via API, and a single flow can only run in one mode at a time.

records.title: Strict-Mode Actors Need a Definition of Done
records.contentHtml: A Strict actor won’t hand off until its Definition of Done is satisfied, so leaving that field blank on a Strict actor can stall the conversation indefinitely. Set a concrete completion rule any time you use Strict focus mode.

records.title: Choose a Focus Mode on Purpose
records.contentHtml: Auto, Flexible, Persistent, and Strict each change how eagerly an actor hands off when the user changes topics. Use Flexible for thin triage agents, Persistent for multi-step intake that can be resumed, and Strict only for identity, payment, or compliance flows that must not be interrupted.

records.title: Keep Behavior Rules Out of Context
records.contentHtml: Context is inheritable background knowledge; Instructions are private behavior rules that never pass to child actors. Put a rule like “always confirm before sending” into Context instead of Instructions, and every child actor will inherit it and try to do the same job.

records.contentHtml: Describe the triggering situation in plain language on each routing edge, for example “when the user asks about price, plans, or wants an Enterprise quote,” instead of keyword conditions like “intent = billing.” Avoid overlapping activation prompts on sibling edges, since the router will pick one nondeterministically.

records.title: Flows Are Built From Actors, Not Nodes
records.contentHtml: A Conversation Flow has exactly one Start node plus one or more actors connected by routing edges — there’s no separate dispatcher or LLM node to wire up. Each actor holds its own model, prompt, and capabilities, and the Start node just routes new conversations into the first actor.

records.title: Variables Are Critical
records.contentHtml:
If your output appears unstructured and wrapped in {{ }}, it is in JSON format. In many cases, you may want to display plain text instead – adjust the variable input accordingly.
If a variable name contains multiple words or spaces, reference it using square brackets with double quotes.
If a variable name is a single word with no spaces, reference it using dot notation.

For example:

Your name:
{{llm_eating_analyser.structuredOutput[“Name of thelead”1}}

What we will eat in the first course:
{{llm_eating_analyser.structuredOutput[“What wewill eat in the first course”1}}

records.title: HTTP Node: GET
records.contentHtml:
Purpose: Retrieve data

What it does: Requests information from a server

Example: Get a user profile, fetch a list of orders, read data

seo.ogDescription: Purpose: Retrieve data What it does: Requests information from a server Example: Get a user profile, fetch a list of orders, read data

records.title: HTTP Node: POST
records.contentHtml:
Purpose: Create or trigger something

What it does: Sends data to the server to create a new resource or start an action

Example: Create a user, submit a form, trigger a workflow, send a webhook event

seo.ogDescription: Purpose: Create or trigger something What it does: Sends data to the server to create a new resource or start an action Example: Create a user, submit a form, trigger a workflow, send a webhook event

records.title: HTTP Node. CheatSheet
records.contentHtml:
Read data: GET

Create / trigger: POST

Replace fully: PUT

Update partially: PATCH

Delete: DELETE

Check only headers: HEAD

Ask “what can I do here?”: OPTIONS

seo.ogDescription: Read data: GET Create / trigger: POST Replace fully: PUT Update partially: PATCH Delete: DELETE Check only headers: HEAD Ask “what can I do here?”: OPTIONS
